intro:
Brutalist architecture uses exposed, unpainted concrete or brick, as an ethic of honest materials as much as a look. Swedish architect Hans Asplund coined the word nybrutalism for a brick house in Uppsala designed in 1950. Alison Smithson first printed "new brutalism" in 1953, and the critic Reyner Banham used it in a 1955 essay to name both an ethic and a style. The name is often traced to béton brut, Le Corbusier's phrase for his rough concrete. The style spread around the world, and its popularity began to fall in the late 1970s.

Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation in Marseille (1952) is often cited as the style's first inspiration: a vertical neighbourhood of duplex flats served by internal streets. Park Hill in Sheffield (1961) takes those streets outside as wide concrete decks that follow the slope. Boston City Hall (1968) is an inverted ziggurat whose form shows the city government's work from outside. The Kenyatta International Convention Centre in Nairobi (1973) sets a cylindrical tower beside a conical-roofed hall. The Barbican Centre in London (1982) buries an arts centre below a podium of walkways, lakes and bush-hammered towers.

intro:
Museum architecture has to keep a collection safe and open it to the public, and every museum building strikes its own balance between the two. The word museum goes back to a Greek place dedicated to the Muses. Museums began as private collections; in France, the Louvre in Paris became the first public museum. Some museums move into old buildings that have outlived their use; others marry a new wing to an old one. Cities have also used museums as tools for economic growth.

The Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York (1959), called a landmark of 20th-century architecture, replaces floors and rooms with one continuous spiral ramp around a skylit atrium. I. M. Pei's Louvre Pyramid in Paris (1989) lights an underground hall that links the museum's wings. Tate Modern in London (2000) turned a power station into a museum, its Turbine Hall an indoor street. Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao (1997) shaped its titanium curves with CATIA, aerospace software, and its pull on the city became known as the Bilbao effect. Study them for how visitors move, where light comes from, and what a museum does for its city.

intro:
London's architecture is worth studying because the city has been rebuilt again and again on its old ground. The Great Fire of 1666, which destroyed about nine tenths of the city, was a turning point. Wren's grid plan was set aside: the city was rebuilt on its medieval streets, under a 1667 act asking for brick houses of uniform height and plot size. Pevsner praised Wren's dome for St Paul's as among the most perfect in the world. Most of the city walls came down in the 18th century so London could grow; Victorian London built the world's first underground railway. John Nash laid out Regent Street with James Burton and remodelled Buckingham House into Buckingham Palace.

The Palace of Westminster (1876), by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin, wraps the parliament in Perpendicular Gothic Revival detail. Battersea Power Station (1955) is one of the world's largest brick buildings. The Barbican Estate (1982) lifts housing, arts and a lake onto walkways above the street. The Lloyd's Building (1986) sets its lifts, stairs and ducts in plug-in towers around a 60-metre atrium. The Shard (2012) became London's first supertall skyscraper.

intro:
Adaptive reuse gives an existing building a new purpose instead of pulling it down. It avoids the cost of demolition and keeps the energy already spent on the original building. An old building can also be mined for materials for new projects, and it keeps a community's link to its past. The usual hurdles are structure and building codes, so a condition survey decides whether a project works.

The Musée d'Orsay in Paris (1986) fills a former railway station, whose glazed barrel vault now shelters stepped stone gallery terraces. Lina Bo Bardi's SESC Pompéia in São Paulo (1986) keeps a drum factory as a leisure centre and adds concrete towers linked by bridges. Tate Modern in London (2000) turned a power station into a gallery, and its Turbine Hall became an indoor street. The High Line in New York (2009) is a park on an abandoned elevated railway. Zeitz MOCAA in Cape Town (2017) carves a grain silo into an atrium shaped like a single grain of corn. These adaptive reuse examples show what to keep and where a new cut can open the old structure.

intro:
Parametric architecture designs buildings with algorithms: the architect sets input parameters, and the model changes as they change. Patrik Schumacher coined the term parametricism in 2008 and described it as a successor to modernism and postmodernism. In it, every element of a design can vary and adapt to the others. It rejects both serial repetition and a heap of unrelated pieces, aiming for complex space that stays legible. Its early practitioners included Greg Lynn, Jesse Reiser, Lars Spuybroek and Kas Oosterhuis. Grasshopper, built on Rhino, is a visual programming tool for such models.

Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao (1997) came before the name, its titanium curves drawn with CATIA, aerospace software. UNStudio's Mercedes-Benz Museum in Stuttgart (2006) winds double-helix ramps on a trefoil plan. Zaha Hadid's MAXXI in Rome (2010) braids concrete galleries under a roof of light fins, and her Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku (2012) folds one continuous surface from plaza to roof, with no line between wall and ground. Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport Terminal 3 (2013), by Studio Fuksas, wraps a 1.6 km terminal in a double honeycomb skin pierced by hexagonal openings.
